It is logical, however, that the meaning of the sentence has the presentation of word-meanings as its intermediate operation; for that [sentence] is not itself the instrument.
Indeed, it is the words in their syntactic connection that constitute the instrument, not the connection itself.

Even so, if it is argued that the words possess a coherence (*saṅgati*) conducive to the demonstration of that [relation], we say no; for coherence does not serve as a basis for the demonstration of the sentence-meaning,
because it has either only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, or only that which possesses the universal (*tadvat*) as its object.
Nor can it be [the agent] by virtue of possessing an activity conducive to that [action],
for it has already been stated that it is not an instrument (*karaṇa*).
We have no dispute regarding its being conducive to that [action] insofar as it instigates the activity of the instrument which is conducive to it.

If it is argued that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in what is already connected, it has been stated in this regard that this is untenable because the meaning of the sentence is something previously unknown (*apūrva*) and because the sequence of cognition would be impossible.

[Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, *Ślokavārttika* 3.376]. There is a connection between a case-role (*kāraka*) when it is connected with a remembered action, and an action when it is connected with a remembered case-role;
therefore, there is no room for the aforementioned defect.
Nor does it follow that they are mere synonyms,
because they are restricted by their primary significance;
nor is there any tautology.
This is because the intention lies in the connection with a specific [property];
nor is there the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*),
since there is no requirement for the recollection of its own meaning [prior to the cognition of the qualifier].

Nor does there arise the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), because when the recollections of the mutual word-meanings are present, there is no dependence on anything else. If this is argued, we reply: No. What is the meaning of the statement "the apprehension of the relation [of a word] is with respect to the related"?
If it means that wherever the relation exists, that thing is, by the nature of reality, a related word-meaning; [then...]
This is not at all relevant to the present topic;

for it is not the case that whatever the capacity of the eye is understood to have, that object must necessarily possess tangibility by way of its actual nature, nor is such possession [of tangibility] its [the eye's] object.
Now, if the meaning is that the linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) regarding that [word] consists precisely in its being connected [to other words], that is incorrect,
because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [for it].
If it is argued that this is established by the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the comprehension of the connected meaning, we say no.

Since the [cognition of meaning] is established even by the theory of the expression of the unconnected (*ananvitābhidhāna*), let there be no inconsistency regarding expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For it is not the case that, when a general connection is not apprehended, there would be a desire to know a specific connection; rather, this is established even through implication (*ākṣepa*), just as one might desire to know a specific taste once a specific fruit has been seen.
If it is argued that— since the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) would otherwise occur among objects remembered from any source whatsoever even in the absence of the greatness of words,
and yet this is not the case—
the power of words must necessarily be postulated— then from what source do the poetic compositions of poets flourish?
For there is no such thing as the composition of a sentence without perceiving a particular relation [between words];

nor, in one's own creative imagination, can perception, inference, verbal testimony, or their fallacies possibly occur, except through the recollection of word-meanings brought about by the force of contemplation.
If it is argued that this is merely a non-apprehension of non-connection, for me, at least, it is indeed an apprehension of connection.
For you as well, that same series of words culminates in a certain relation.
If it is argued that there is sometimes no apprehension of the positive concomitance (anvaya), from what specific distinction does this arise?
If you say it is due to whether the speaker is trustworthy (āpta) or untrustworthy (anāpta), then has some specific quality been imparted to the object by such a speaker?
Or is the distinction [between the two views] due to the speaker acting as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*)?
In the first case, there is the same burden of postulating a linguistic potency (*śakti*) for you as there is for the proponents of *abhihitānvaya*.
In the second case, let the words themselves, like the speaker, possess the capacity to differentiate by virtue of being delimiting factors.
If that is so, then words also have utility in the cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*);
what doubt could there be? It is simply by means of the expression of word-meanings (*padārtha*).
But it is not otherwise, as in your own view,
where [the meaning arises] merely from the juxtaposition of words through the intention of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) directed toward a connection.
But it is not otherwise.

Otherwise, this verse should have been recited by those who know the opinions of the teachers (gurumata), having inserted the word "āpta" [in place of "śabda"]: "Because of being primary, because of being the expresser, and also because of the acceptance of intentionality, that capacity should preferably be admitted as belonging to the authorities (āptas) alone."
Thus it is said.

Therefore, whether the cognition of relation occurs through some other means or not, since the word-meanings possess expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, there is necessarily a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) once they have been denoted; how then can there be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of this principle]?
And it is not the case that, this being so, the word-meanings themselves are the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Since it is impossible for those [past and future things] to function as causal agents by virtue of having a form such as the future and so forth, it is illogical for their specific property of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) to exist;
furthermore, there is an absence of any example of their connection [with a result] that is not conflated with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
However, in the case of words, this is possible because they necessarily precede [the cognition], possessing the intermediate operation of recollecting the word-meanings.
Since activity does not constitute an intervention, enough of this digression.
Let it be then that sound itself is the sublater regarding an omniscient creator.
For instance: "All actions are performed in every way by the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti)."
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."
They recite [the verse] beginning with "g.ī. and so forth.
Its meaning is this: the agency of the conscious being does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality;
rather, it is merely a matter of conceit (*ābhimānika*).

Furthermore, there is no conceit in one who is omniscient, nor is there world-authorship for one who is not omniscient—it is said in response: "The word of one who is not authoritative is not a means of valid cognition; nor is there authoritativeness in anyone regarding what is unperceived.
An omniscient being is not established through the perception of the imperceptible, and an eternal scripture is not tenable. (16)

For if the word that does not indicate the absence of an omniscient author is not spoken by a reliable person (āpta), then it is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). But if its speaker is a reliable person, [then it is a means of valid cognition].
How is it that he does not perceive that object?
If you say, "Because he perceives objects beyond the senses," then how is he not omniscient,
or how is he not the creator?
This is because [the scripture] is merely composed;
furthermore, the existence of an eternal scripture is impossible, as it has already been explained that there is a break in its transmission.
Furthermore: Nor is this [nature] absolute in any respect, because existence is also perceived;
nor is it solely intent upon the realization of the stainless, even though that exists. (17)
For the scripture is not restricted solely to the side of non-existence,
since the existence of Īśvara is established in many places;
as we shall demonstrate further on.
This being the case, the demonstration of non-existence in some instances is not a subverting factor for the [doctrine of] non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
If it is argued that, by parity of reasoning, the demonstration of existence is likewise not a proof—this may indeed be so from a superficial standpoint;

however, when it is determined that the purpose of the scriptures on authorlessness (*akartṛkatva*) is to demonstrate the nature of the Self as devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), [the matter becomes clear].
"In that case, since their intention is not to negate that [soul], the authority will belong only to those scriptures that establish its existence.
We shall explain later that even for those [scriptures], the intention does not lie elsewhere.
"Well then, let presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) be the sublater."
For instance: if it were [already] existent, he would not have taught it;
for he does not fail to know how to set it forth without having first taught it.

Therefore, it is not the case that the very fact that the instruction is otherwise inexplicable makes known the non-existence or the indifference toward such [an object]; for it is explicable in another way:
"Since there is no effect in the absence of a cause, there is no valid cognition when the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is absent;
due to its absence, there is no activity. This same rule applies even in the doctrine of karma. (18)
For an activity preceded by intelligence cannot be accomplished without first producing that intelligence;
nor can even that intelligence be established in the present case without instruction, since instruction alone is its cause.

If it is argued that one should set [the mind] in motion according to the principle of possession by a spirit (*bhūtāveśanyāya*), then indeed one might so set it in motion, provided that the result were achieved in that manner;
however, it is not so.
How is this determined? Precisely by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the instruction.
Even in the view of one for whom the activity of the elements occurs solely by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), [the same conclusion follows].
This is equally true for that [other view] as well:
if there exists an unseen cause for its occurrence, what is the use of instruction?
For activity is established from that very [source] alone.
If it were not so, then what would be the use of instruction?
Because even when that [instruction] exists, there would be no activity in its absence.

If it is argued that an eternal and independent teaching is not subject to questioning, then you yourselves are the ones who ought to be questioned, for you are those who, with focused attention, uphold and investigate it.

Nor is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) distinct from inference (*anumāna*), because there is no example in the world where the two are unmixed, and because there is no other possible mode [of relation].
For it is said: "That which is not constrained cannot be logically impossible, nor can that which is not a constraint be a subsumer (*upapādaka*)."
There is no contradiction between the two measures; or even if they were well-known, that [contradiction] would be the same.
They cite as an example: "Caitra, being alive, is not in the house"— this being logically untenable in the absence of his presence outside, leads one to infer it.
In this regard, it is considered: what is untenable about the absence from home of one who is alive?
For nothing is untenable for that which lacks a restrictive rule without a restrictor, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Is it not simply its own nature?
That [nature] cannot first be produced by way of external existence,
because that [external existence] is not something to be produced by it.

If it is argued that its very nature (*svabhāva*) is such that it could not exist without that [cause], and therefore its stability is [dependent on it]—then in that case, this [effect] would have a nature strictly determined by that [cause];
for it is precisely the pervasion (*vyāpti*), when defined through the method of negation (*vyatireka-mukha*), that is designated in such a manner.
Or else, how...?
Is external existence the probans for this [internal existence]?
For even that which is unconditioned does not establish what is unconditioned,
precisely because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that its nature is such that, by virtue of being an external existence, it must remain while embracing the absence from the house— this is simply the very pervasion (*vyāpti*) defined from the perspective of positive concomitance (*anvaya-mukha*), and is designated as such.
We do not deny the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
But if it is argued that this cognition [of non-existence] does not,
by its mere existence, bring about the status of being an inference for that [non-existence], we say no; for one must necessarily admit the connection with the non-occurrence [of the reason],
otherwise there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And because there is no room for fallacious presumptive testimony (*arthāpattyābhāsa*);
for when one considers that something which is established in one way is nonetheless inexplicable otherwise, [it is not a valid presumption].
In that case, there is its negation, but not otherwise.
If it is asked, "Even so, how is pervasion (vyāpti) apprehended here?"—[the answer is: when I am here, then I am not elsewhere.
That "when it is elsewhere, then it is not here" is unestablished by any direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); what uncertainty (*kathantā*) could there be even in that regard?
Furthermore, it is not the case that because all locations are imperceptible, its absence therein is difficult to ascertain.
This is because their conjunction is denied in the self.

If it is asked, "What is the status regarding the denial of those [atoms] that are incapable [of conjunction]?"—the answer is: it follows by inference precisely from the denial of their conjunction with those [parts], since they are the constituent parts of them; for others, there is no such [denial].
For it is not possible to determine that "this is not conjoined with an atom" by means of an atom that has not become a cause.

Nor is it logical to claim that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is that which makes something known through the ascertainment of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), even if it is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); for this would entail the consequence that being a property of the subject is not a necessary condition, as there would be no distinction [between such cases and other types of inference].

Furthermore, because it is impossible to ascertain an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between two things that reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), since the formulation "whatever [is] where [and] when" is untenable.
When there is a contradiction between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) serves to establish their non-contradiction.
But it is not the case that there is no such thing as inference either;
for in the event of a contradiction, as in the case of a rope-snake and the like, there would simply be the sublation of one,
and not the validity of both.
Alternatively, there is no contradiction regarding their validity,
because they can coexist— just as in the case of "this is one large [object]"—
or because their objects are distinct, just as in the case of "this is Caitra" and "this is Maitra."

If it is argued that because [the term] "somewhere" is used in its general sense, there is also a commonality of referent since the house is included [among those places], then if this is so, there is no contradiction, just as in the case of saying "it exists somewhere" and "it does not exist somewhere.
If you say that here too there is indeed a contradiction, then one of the two must necessarily be abandoned.
If it is argued that [the contradiction] would not apply because both [positions] are established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), then what is it that is unaccountable?

If you say that the contradiction itself, being otherwise unaccountable, establishes [the two positions] by assigning them to different domains, then why does it not establish them precisely as having the same domain?
Establishment is the bringing about of non-contradiction.

And since the contradiction between these two exists precisely because they have the same object, how can that [contradiction] be pacified by that very same [object]? For one who has fainted from the poison of a particular thing cannot be cured by that very same thing.
If it is argued that "it is raised up by that very [same thing]," then from what does this contradiction between these two follow on the basis of having a single object?
If it is argued that "it is because they are always perceived as having distinct locations and natures," then surely this is a pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And so, at the very threshold of the argument—(204)
"It is dawn.
Or rather, even smoke would lead one to infer fire precisely because it is otherwise inexplicable;
for without that [fire], this [smoke] cannot be accounted for.
There is also contradiction: "From smoke, fire must exist," yet "from non-perception, it must not exist.
And thus, there is the establishment of the near side based on non-perception.

Furthermore, since smoke has as its object a fire that is not perceived due to an intervening obstruction, its status as a subject of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) would follow; so how could there be inference?
The inference "this [place] possesses fire" arises from pervasion (*vyāpti*);
otherwise, in the absence of inference, contradiction (*virodha*) could not be established.

If it is argued that the statement "there is fire on its far side" is merely a presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) because it is contradicted by the non-perception of fire on the near side—this is not so; for the contradiction has already been stated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Nor is the latter a presumptive testimony;
otherwise, the establishment of being a *pālāla* tree through the contradiction between being white and not being a *pālāla* would also have to be considered merely a presumptive testimony.

If it is argued that this is not the case because there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that which is qualified by it [the fire] by that very [fire], then if this were so, how could it be otherwise? For smoke qualified by the state of having fire unperceived on its near side is likewise pervaded by that very [fire]; thus, the two cases are equal.

If it is argued that the inference of the purely negative type (*kevalavyatirekin*), as accepted by others, is actually "presumption" (*arthāpatti*) because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), we do not deny the application of the term "presumption" to such an inference on account of this specific distinction alone.
If it is asked why the application of the term "inference" is used there, it is because it arises from a mark (*liṅga*) that is inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*).

For the non-occurrence [of the probans] in the absence of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is no different for a negative-only (vyatirekin) inference than it is for a positive (anvayin) one; and its ascertainment occurs either through both positive and negative concomitance or through one or the other.
Therefore, "presumption" (arthāpatti) is merely a synonym for inference (anumāna).

Or rather, it is logical that the statement regarding its specific nature is "like the previous" and so forth; however, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) has already been considered not to be a sublater (*bādhikā*),
nor does it exceed the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of valid cognition.

That is stated as follows: Because the cognition is immediate, because the sense organ is not exhausted, because it is an instrument of unknown [perception], and because of the mind's immersion in the object. (20)
For whatever cognition is direct perception is produced by the sense organs,
just like the cognition of color and so forth.

Likewise, regarding the cognition "there is no jar here on the ground," if it is argued that its status as a direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*) is unestablished, we say no; for if two cognitions belong to the same class, it is impossible for them to function as instruments of knowledge in one case when known and in the other when unknown.
Indeed, in the case of a single effect, the very same instrument cannot be employed at one time when known and at another time when unknown.
Furthermore, this would entail the undesirable consequence of the reversal of the roles of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and the sense faculty (*indriya*),
as well as the consequence that cognition would lack a cause;
for it is not the case that something can be the cause of another even when it is bypassed, as that would involve a contradiction.

Therefore, since that which is produced by the non-apprehension of a known object possesses direct perceptuality (*sākṣātkāritva*), it is logical that this [present cognition], having causes contrary to that, belongs to a different class from it.
But where, indeed, does the non-apprehension of a known object produce a cognition of absence that lacks direct perceptuality? For example: "I have searched very thoroughly for Caitra in the house."
Nor does the hearer infer from the hearing of the word "not perceived" that "surely it did not exist at all"; by this,
its prior non-existence is also explained.
If it is objected: "Even so, let there be a distinction of intermediate classes;

however, how can there be direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) produced by non-apprehension of the unknown?"—it has already been stated that there must be a contradiction in the effect due to the contradiction in the cause.
Furthermore, [direct perception] arises immediately after the operation of the sense organ, which is not exhausted elsewhere.

If it is argued that [the cognition of absence] is exhausted by the apprehension of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), we say no; for even a blind person would then have the cognition of the absence of color in a jar or similar object presented to them by the sense of touch, since he possesses the apprehension of the locus and the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Indeed, he has the apprehension of the locus, and he also has the recollection of the counter-positive.
[Objection: There is both the absence and the non-apprehension of the dark-red color that is fit [to be perceived];

and this is the same even for one who maintains that an absence is apprehended by the very sense organ that apprehends the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). [Reply: No, because [we] accept that an absence is apprehended by the sense organ that apprehends its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). [Objection:

For me as well, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is non-apprehension when the locus has been grasped by the sense organ that apprehends the counter-positive. [Reply: No, because it would follow that the cognition of the absence of color would not arise in the case of air when it is presented to the tactile sense organ (*tvagindriya*).

If it is argued that even so, that [absence] is proximate there—well then, in this case, the sense organ, which has its function fulfilled nowhere else, must necessarily be depended upon for the experience of the absence of color.

It might be argued: "Even so, its utility lies precisely in the apprehension of another object. If this is said, we reply: no, because that [other object] is not a cause with respect to that [apprehension of absence].
Or, if it were a cause, one would not perceive the absence of a tangible substance through the touch of a hand in deep darkness.
And one would perceive the lack of blackness in the object situated behind while having the eyes wide open toward the front.

If it is argued that the upright position of the substratum is also required [for perception], then the contact of the eye with the object will likewise be required, since it depends upon the contact with light as its specific auxiliary cause; [as stated in the verse: "the window... (205).
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving that object even in a location touched by a hand that spreads through an opening;
for in such a case, the eye is already exhausted in producing the capacity [for perception].
Indeed, the non-existence of something not being perceived is ascertained only when all other conditions of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) are present.
If it is argued that this [cognition] would occur when the eye is in proximity to a substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—but surely, completeness (*sākalya*) consists precisely in the causes being fully present;
and if so, what is lacking, and where? Or is it the mutual conjunction [of the causes]? (207)
If that which is expressed by terms such as "mutual proximity" (mithaḥ-pratyāsatti) were the object of its [the sense organ's] exhaustion,
then the eye would never be a cause [of perception];
for it does not produce even the apprehension of color-form (rūpa) and so forth when it is not in contact [with the object].
[Ku. 3.399] Furthermore, even the perception of something inherent in a locus must depend upon non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) for the apprehension of the absence of that object;
therefore, in that case, this [non-perception] has fulfilled its purpose.
However, in the case of air and so forth, the cognition of the absence of color and other qualities is inferential (*ānumānikī*).
Likewise, it is not the case that air is inferred to be formless on the basis of non-apprehension; for this is unestablished,
since for you [the Yogācārins], the absence of apprehension is not itself an apprehension of non-existence.
Because it is admitted that apprehension (*upalambha*) is beyond the reach of the senses.

If it is argued that [the object] is inferable due to the absence of manifestness (*prākaṭya*), we say no; for even the absence of manifestness of color in air is unestablished, since it is the same as the case of the absence of color itself.

If it is argued that [the existence of such knowledge] is to be inferred from the absence of linguistic usage, we say no—because even in the absence of physical or vocal activity, the presence of a state of indifferent cognition (*upekṣājñāna*) is admitted;
furthermore, this is established by the occurrence of mute dreams.
Moreover, it is not even possible to infer [such knowledge] merely on the basis of the absence of linguistic usage.
Because it is inconclusive and because it is unestablished; however,
conventional usage regarding that object is either produced by the cognition of that object or produces the cognition of that object.
Or [it might be] that which produces the dharma which is its support;
yet the absence of that [dharma] is necessarily included within the absence of that cognition and its supporting dharma, and thus its non-existence is simply impossible to ascertain.
This is because it would entail the fallacies of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), and circularity (*cakraka*).
Nor can the non-apprehension of that which is unknown serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the absence of manifestation (*prākaṭyābhāva*) makes known the absence of apprehension by its mere existence; for if the absence of a logical mark were to function in such a way, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If, however, there were a restriction based on the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), then one would have to admit the necessity of perceiving that concomitance.
For invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) does not determine the cause of cognition by its mere existence, because otherwise it would follow that smoke and the like would also possess such a status.

If it is argued that it will occur through the perceptibility of the cognition according to your own direction, we say no; for the answer has already been stated regarding the destruction of sound and so forth.

Furthermore, it must be established— either by the force of pervasion or because its effect would otherwise be erratic— that for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) to be a valid means of knowledge, the cognition of the property of the locus (*adhikaraṇadharma*) by the same sense faculty that apprehends the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a necessary factor; for if that were lacking, such non-apprehension would deviate from its intended result.
First of all, non-apprehension in the form described above is not observed to fail to produce the cognition of absence without that [non-existence];
nor does it follow from pervasion, for if that were the case, the cognition of the absence of color in fire would entail that [non-existence].
Because it is thus constituted;
or, in the absence of projection, it would not have that as its cause.
Or it might not exist at all;
if you argue that it therefore simply does not exist, [we reply: is not that very same thing also the probans?
It is not a different reality;

just as the relationship by birth depends upon the contact of the sense organs during the state of being unmarked (*aliṅga*), whereas in the state of being marked (*liṅga*), it does not depend on that at all for the knowledge of Brahminhood.
If it is argued that this may be so, we say no— because such a distinction is possible due to the difference in the classes of effects (*kāryajātibheda*),
and because that [distinction] is not admitted in the present case.
If it is argued that this [distinction] will exist otherwise even while setting aside mediacy (*pārokṣya*) and immediacy (*apārokṣya*), we say no— because it is not perceived (*anupalambha*).
If it is argued that it is at least possible— let it be possible;
however, even on this basis, there can be no determination of the restriction of the instrument (karaṇa),
because the instrument remains unknown.
Knowledge produced by a means that is not itself cognized is directly produced by the sense organ,
just as the perception of color is;
and such is the knowledge here that "there is no jar on this ground."
Or, just as memory— which arises directly from the mind without its instrument being known— is not of the nature of a direct experience,
why then is it not a direct perception?
We shall explain that this is because there is no sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) other than the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
[Objection: Even so, this rule applies only to the domain of positive entities (*bhāva*);

however, the cognition of a non-entity (*abhāva*), even if its instrument is unknown, will not be directly produced by the sense organs. [Response: This is not so—because a general rule cannot be restricted in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
Otherwise, it would follow that all pervasions (*vyāpti*) would have only positive entities as their objects, since there is no distinction [between them].
If it is asked, "Even so, what is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-position?"—well, this very one is it.
Listen also to another that is being stated:
namely, the consequence of an effect arising without a cause.
Alternatively, it would follow that even the perceptions of form and so forth must have something other than the sense organs as their instruments;
for the establishment of the eyes and other organs does not occur on the basis of perceptions such as inference, which are produced by instruments other [than the senses].
Rather, it is by means of the very perceptions of form and so forth, whose instruments are not perceived, that [the sense organs are inferred].
Although the quality of being a direct perception (sākṣātkāritā) also ultimately culminates in that very same [inference],
nevertheless, at the outset, the fact of having an unperceived instrument is the sole motivator for postulating the eye and the other senses.
For if another instrument were perceived, no one would have postulated the eye and so forth as being unperceived even when those [cognitions] are direct perceptions.
For this very reason, the wise have accepted that the mind alone is the instrument of memory, even though it is not a direct perception;
the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), however, serves to bring about proximity to the specific object.
Because it has been established that the sense-faculties function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*),
and because the mind is permeated by the existence [of the object]:

for whenever the experience of an external object is to be produced, the mind must necessarily be permeated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has become an existent entity (*bhāvabhūta*).
"There is no other way" constitutes the pervasion (vyāpti),
because the capacity is determined in that very manner;
for that [capacity], when accompanied by mere non-perception, is not able to produce an experience even in the case of absence.
Because we observe the dependence [of cognition] upon words, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth;

and it is not logically tenable that something which is observed to be the producer of a certain effect only when dependent upon something else could be the producer of that very same effect independently of that thing.
For otherwise, there would be the contingency of smoke arising from fire even in the absence of a connection with moist fuel;
and thus, one would have abandoned the laborious pursuit of grasping the relationship between cause and effect.
Furthermore: "Because of its capacity toward the counter-positive, and because there is no intervention by an operation..."
Because defects have the sense-faculties as their basis, and because [the latter] are subject to conceptual construction. //21//

For whatever means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apprehends the existence of a certain thing, that very same means apprehends the non-existence of its opposite, just as a logical mark (liṅga) or a word (śabda).
And the sense faculty apprehends [objects] such as a jar;
otherwise, it would not even indicate the absence of sound and so forth,
since its capacity is determined only with respect to a positive entity (bhāva).
Nor is this alone reasonable;

for from the statement "Devadatta is not in the house," there is also an understanding through inference based on non-perception, as realized by the thought: "Even though I was seeking him there, Maitra was not seen by me."
Or, let the sense-faculty apprehend the locus; even so, this [object] is not obstructed by it,
because [the faculty] is merely an operation.
Otherwise, one would be pouring water on the head of all conceptual cognitions by granting them the status of perception.

[Objection: If this were so, then the apprehension of smoke would also be an operation (*vyāpāra*) of this [perception], and thus inference too would be rendered obsolete. [Reply: This is not so; for when a certain causal status cannot be established without a particular action, that action is considered its operation.
Because that very [perception] is the operation (*vyāpāra*) directed toward that [object].
Nor is it the case that the eye's status as a cause for the cognition of fire cannot be established without the perception of smoke and so forth, as is the case with conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Furthermore, there is indeed a reversal of presence and absence.
Therefore, it is logical that whatever defect this [non-apprehension] follows is precisely what constitutes the instrument here;
and non-apprehension is not defective by its very nature.
Nor is the apprehension of the locus or the recollection of the counter-positive inherently defective;
for it does not fail to arise at the time of its non-arising,
and at the time of its arising, its nature of illuminating its own object remains unaltered.

If it is argued that it is defective to perceive two things that are non-conjoined and non-correlative as being conjoined, and likewise to perceive two things that are conjoined as being non-conjoined— well, this is precisely the error of *viparyaya* (misapprehension).
And thus, there is the fault of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Therefore, just as a defective sense organ has the capacity to produce its opposite [an erroneous cognition], so too a non-defective one has the capacity to produce a correct cognition of that same object.
And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*): A sense organ is the instrument for the valid cognition of absence, because it is the instrument for the cognition of its opposite;
whatever is the instrument for the cognition of the opposite of X is the instrument for the valid cognition of X.
Just as the eye is the instrument for the cognition of form,
so too, because of conceptualization:
indeed, the specific cognition that "the ground is devoid of a jar" must necessarily be admitted to have the sense faculty as its instrument.
Or else, a seventh means of valid cognition must be admitted.

For just as the sense organ, being exhausted by the mere substantive (viśeṣya), is not the instrument here, so too non-apprehension, being exhausted by the mere qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), would not be the instrument.

If it is argued that the cause is the conjunction of two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) each operating solely upon its own respective object, we say no; for such a conjunction is untenable when the objects differ and the resulting effects are of different kinds.
Indeed, there can be no conjunction of a potter and a weaver while they are engaged with clay and threads respectively;
nor is the conjunction of the wheel, the loom, and other tools used by the makers of jars, cloth, and so forth, of any utility anywhere.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is not like that in the former case because there is no variegated effect (*karburakārya*), whereas in the present case it is like that because we observe a qualified cognition consisting of both perceptual and non-perceptual forms—[we reply: no, because there is no co-inherence of contradictory universals (*viruddhajāti*);
or, if such co-inherence did exist, it would be a variegated (*karambita*) whole.
Thus, the capacity for both [causes] must be admitted regarding the effect,
on the strength of observation;
for an effect characterized by variegation cannot be established by a capacity restricted to a single object.
Otherwise, the same undesirable consequence would apply elsewhere as well.

If it is objected, "If both [qualities] possess the capacity for both [objects], what is the purpose of their mutual proximity?", we say no; for that [quality] possesses its capacity there only when conjoined with the other.
By this, expressions such as "fragrant sandalwood" are explained.

Thus, since the capacity of the sense organs with respect to non-existence is difficult to deny, enough with this attachment to what is unreal. It might be argued: "A cognition of a qualified object does not arise when the qualifier has not been apprehended, because it is the effect of that [apprehension]."
Nor does the capacity [of the sense organ] exist in the mere qualifier when it possesses a qualified capacity,
because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the eye functioning even toward mere fragrance.
Therefore, there is the possibility of another means of knowledge for the apprehension of the qualifier which is a non-existence.
Furthermore, how could an object that has not been perceived by the sense organ be conceptually constructed?
Nor is this the method for other means of valid cognition,
since inference and the like construct objects even when they have not been previously perceived.
And because [the object] has not been reached:
for conjunction and so forth with the sense organ are not possible with a non-existent thing;
nor is there the status of being a qualifier.

If it is argued that this is because [the non-existence of the object] is preceded by another relation, and because non-perception must necessarily be admitted—since the perception of its absence does not occur while that [object] is being perceived—[we reply: it is said in response: (210)

If [it is argued that] because the apprehension of a delimitation is stable, [the object] is not unstable, then this proves what is already established; if [it is argued that] there is no instability because of another attainment, then there is an infinite regress, and thus even the other [case] is difficult to maintain. //22//
For that [object], while about to become a qualifier of another object, might manifest even in its isolated state, provided that the cognition which delimits it is not its manifestor;
and that [object] is perceived as something to be conceptualized (*vikalpya*).
That which is made known by a sense faculty independently of the cognition of a qualifier,

but which appears only preceded by that [qualifier], does not fall under this rule, because its capacity exists only when there is the convergence of the causal complex for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Even when there is attainment through intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), an additional attainment is accepted for form and so forth by the power of realization (*pratipatti*). However, in this case, such acceptance is not made because of the flaw of infinite regress (*anavasthā*);
yet, the proximity of intrinsic nature does not become fruitless merely by this much.
If it were not so,

all of this would be difficult to establish even regarding other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, every means of valid cognition, whether directly or indirectly, ultimately rests upon non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*).
For even inference and the like are not preceded by non-examination;

therefore, how could non-existence be conceptualized even by means of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) if it has not been examined? Nor does that [non-perception] produce the examination of that [object] itself.
Because it is impossible to define that [viśeṣaṇatva] unless it is delimited by a counter-correlate (pratiyogin);
or, if such definition were possible, what would the sense organ have done wrong?
Likewise, because viśeṣaṇatva is necessarily characterized by the inclusion of another relation.
What remedy is there even for another means of knowledge?
For the absence of that [means] is equally present at that time as well.
If it is argued that the other [means] possesses identity with that [object], then surely, if that [identity] exists—
It certainly exists; if it did not, it would not exist at all.
For objects are not brought into being by mere assertion, nor are they negated by non-assertion.
If its necessity of being accepted were established, then its status as a cause would be proven, but not its status as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Otherwise, even upon the perception of a positive entity (*bhāva*), the non-perception of its absence alone would be the means of valid cognition, and not the sense faculty.

Just as there is no perception of an entity when there is the perception of its absence, so too, when there is the perception of an entity, the non-perception of its absence is as indelible as adamantine glue.

(212) Thus, by means of these [means of knowledge] such as direct perception, any arising of contradiction with the lower [levels] is far off; for those who are solely intent on looking at the face [of others], even their own self is not attained.
With surging faith, we take refuge in Him— the God of even the gods— who is compliant with all, who is the one without equal, and for whom the festival of His own sovereign will is a joy. (23)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Nyāyakusumāñjali. //3//
